sources.substrate_plan_design:
## Design

### Architecture

The retrieval substrate gets a clean abstraction. The engine stops doing cosine math; it asks the oracle for nearest chunks under a filter, with sub-linear cost.

rrc.ChunkOracle (interface, in rrc/interfaces.go): ChunksForMessages(ctx, ids) returns a map of message ID to chunk list. EnsureVector(ctx, ref) returns a chunk's embedding, embedding live and persisting through to the cache if not yet stored. NearestChunks(ctx, queryText, k, predicate) returns top-K chunks by cosine to query, restricted to chunks satisfying predicate. The implementation encodes queryText as a query (asymmetric models apply a query-specific prompt; symmetric models encode plainly), then runs an ANN index search (sqlite-vec etc.). Cost is sub-linear in corpus size.

rrc.Predicate (interface, extensible): Apply: predicate compiles to backend-native filter (SQL WHERE, etc.). Concrete predicates (in rrc/predicate.go): PredAll matches every chunk. PredThread matches chunks whose owning thread equals ThreadID. PredScope encodes the user-visible retrieval scope: with Scope = ScopeThread, matches chunks from CurrentThread; with Scope = ScopeAll, matches chunks from any thread. PredAnd matches chunks satisfying every child predicate. PredOr matches chunks satisfying at least one child predicate. PredNot matches chunks that do not satisfy Inner. PredHasMetadata matches chunks whose metadata Key equals Value. The Predicate is a typed AST, not a fixed struct. Backends implement a Compile method that lowers it to whatever the underlying index speaks (SQL clause for sqlite-vec, JSON predicate for vector DBs). Future filters (attached-file presence, role, time-window) add new Pred types without touching the engine or the interface.

### Storage layer: sqlite-vec

The vector index becomes a first-class storage primitive in the SQLite file alongside messages, chunks, scores, edges. Implementation via the sqlite-vec extension. New schema managed by service/storage/migrations: chunk_vectors is a vec0 virtual table keyed by chunk_rowid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY with payload embedding FLOAT[D] where D is the embedder's output dimension. chunk_vector_metadata is a companion regular table indexed alongside chunk_vectors with columns chunk_rowid INTEGER PK, message_id TEXT, chunk_index INTEGER, thread_id TEXT, model_id TEXT, role TEXT, has_attachments BOOL.

The embeddings table is removed in favor of chunk_vectors as the source of truth for vector data. HNSW parameters: vec0 defaults are sane for our scale; tune M=16, ef_construction=200, ef_search=64 initially. Filter integration: NearestChunks lowers the predicate to a SQL WHERE clause that joins chunk_vectors against chunk_vector_metadata and pushes the predicate into the vec0 KNN search. Pre-traversal filtering for high recall rather than post-filter, which collapses recall when the predicate is selective. Concurrency: SQLite WAL handles single-writer/multi-reader. Vector writes happen in the same transaction as the embedding insert.

### Embedder layer

zembed-1 is asymmetric — distinct prompts for queries vs documents, applied automatically by sentence-transformers via model.encode_query and model.encode_document. The current core.Embedder interface is symmetric. Interface change: replace symmetric Embed and EmbedBatch with asymmetric EmbedQuery and EmbedDocument. Engine call sites: the new message being processed embeds via EmbedQuery; chunks being indexed into the corpus embed via EmbedDocument. For symmetric models like bge-m3, the implementation routes both methods to the same code path. Asymmetric is the principled default; symmetric is a degenerate case.

Serving stack: custom Python service. TEI's --default-prompt-name is server-wide, set at boot, not per-request — running asymmetric models would require two TEI containers per embedder. zembed-1's trust_remote_code modeling defines the encode_query/encode_document semantics; vLLM ingests weights and applies its own inference, so it can't faithfully reproduce them. A custom Python service of about 50 LOC plus Dockerfile loads zembed-1 via sentence-transformers, exposes two endpoints /embed/query and /embed/document, routes to model.encode_query and model.encode_document respectively. Single service, single GPU instance, correct semantics by construction.

### Reranker layer

zerank-2 served via vLLM (causal LM serving, OpenAI-compatible API). vLLM exposes per-token logprobs; the Go adapter extracts the Yes token logprob from the completion response and applies sigmoid(logit / 5.0). Prefix KV caching in vLLM is free: scoring N candidates against 1 query reuses the query-prefix's KV state across the N forward passes since the chat-template prefix through user content start is identical across them. vLLM is the principled fit because zerank-2 is a causal LM. Production-grade serving with prefix caching, dynamic batching, paged attention. The reranker swap drops BAAI bge-reranker-v2-m3 and the spidey-tei-rerank-1 Docker container from the production stack.
sources.driver_arc_journal:
## Phase 6: SQLite driver experimentation arc

The plan committed to sqlite-vec but the existing driver (modernc.org/sqlite, pure-Go) doesn't load C extensions. Walked three driver paths:

1. mattn/go-sqlite3 (cgo) plus sqlite-vec-go-bindings/cgo: bindings include sqlite-vec.c that #include sqlite3.h. mattn bundles SQLite via amalgamation but doesn't expose headers to other cgo packages. Build fails: fatal error sqlite3.h No such file or directory.

2. ncruces/go-sqlite3 (WASM, pure-Go) plus sqlite-vec-go-bindings/ncruces: tried v0.34.0 (latest). Fails: undefined sqlite3.Binary. The bindings expect to assign a WASM binary blob to sqlite3.Binary, but recent ncruces releases moved or renamed that symbol.

3. Pin ncruces/go-sqlite3 v0.20.3 (released around the same time as bindings v0.1.6): Binary exists. Combination builds cleanly, storage tests green.

Settled on (3). The embed import had to be dropped — it overwrites sqlite3.Binary with the no-vec build and breaks vec0. The bindings auto-init replaces it with a vec0-included WASM. Order of imports matters; left a comment in db.go pinning the constraint.

Brief rabbit hole: when this stack of driver/binding versions was still failing, I considered hand-rolling HNSW in Go (~300 LOC). User correctly pushed back: 'is there a sqlite library for it or something. not some rando' — pulled me out of the rabbit hole back to the established sqlite-vec path with proper version pinning.

## Phase 7: Storage schema migration to vec0

db.go schema gets: chunk_vectors as a vec0 virtual table with embedding FLOAT[2560] (zembed native dim), aux columns +message_id, +chunk_index, +thread_id, +model_id, +role. Aux columns push predicate filters into the KNN search (pre-traversal, not post-filter — recall preservation).

chunk_vector_rowids: companion table, chunk_rowid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, UNIQUE on (message_id, chunk_index, model_id). Source of truth for vec0 rowid assignment. Eliminates the FNV-1a hash collision risk (10^-5 at 10M rows would still violate non-lossy).

trg_cv_cascade_chunks: AFTER DELETE ON chunks trigger that cleans both vec0 and the rowid mapping. Without it, chunks delete but vector rows persist → orphans show up in top-K KNN, displacing real candidates → silent recall hole.

## The 'unsafe use of virtual table' fight

First trigger attempt failed: sqlite3: SQL logic error: unsafe use of virtual table chunk_vectors. SQLite's default-since-3.31 'untrusted schema' mode forbids triggers from writing to virtual tables (security: prevents tainted attached DBs from running arbitrary code). For a single-application self-owned DB, trusted is appropriate.

Fix: add _pragma=trusted_schema(ON) to the DSN. Trigger fires correctly. Comment in db.go documents the security tradeoff and why trusted is the right mode here.

Initial framing of the workaround was wrong. I called orphan-vector accumulation 'acceptable per RRC's invariance design (storage grows linearly; per-step compute stays bounded)'. User pushed back. The real failure mode wasn't storage growth — it was silent recall loss: orphan vectors take up top-K slots in vec0 KNN results, displacing real candidates, and the engine's downstream filter just drops them without backfill. Recall hole, no signal. Trigger is load-bearing for correctness, not just for tidiness.
sources.claude_md_principles:
# Spidey — Design Methodology

Principles this codebase commits to.

## UI

### Tool outputs render in their tool's slot

A tool call has exactly one home: its own collapsible in the conversation. Every tool output — the Bash stdout, the FileRead content, the pending question from AskUserQuestion, the plan from ExitPlanMode — belongs inside that slot. Nothing floats. Why: a floating card elsewhere adds associative cost. The user has to see the card, figure out which tool call it matches, scroll to that tool call, scroll back to answer. Interactive outputs aren't a different category from static ones; they're the same output with a richer renderer.

### Don't duplicate the chrome

Thread name shows in one place (topbar). Agent running status shows in one place (composer status strip). If a piece of chrome appears twice it's duplication — kill the weaker instance. A thread header with the same name the topbar already shows is noise.

## State

### Write on commit, not on intent

Clicking 'New' shouldn't create a DB thread. The thread materialises on first successful send. Dead threads — created by users who clicked New and walked away — accumulate otherwise. Same principle anywhere else a click could commit to backend state before the user has actually committed. Implementation: /thread/new is a draft URL. ThreadPage detects it, renders a composer with no corpus, and creates the thread on first onSend or onStartAutonomous before navigating to the real id.

### Backend rejections mustn't strand UI

If the user answers a stale question and the backend rejects the mutation (already answered, timeout expired, runner restarted), the dismiss still happens client-side. The user's intent takes precedence over the backend's knowledge. Mutation errors get logged; they don't propagate into stuck UI state.

## Security

### Sandbox is a security boundary, not a UX affordance

When sandboxed=true, every file tool and shell goes through the container. Path tools (FileRead, FileWrite, FileEdit, NotebookEdit) must route through sandbox.ResolveWorkspacePath before any os.ReadFile / os.WriteFile. Bash goes through sandbox.Sandbox. Nothing escapes. The sandbox exists to contain prompt injection — a model tricked into reading id_rsa or writing to /etc/passwd. A split where Bash is sandboxed but FileWrite runs on the host defeats that.

### Fail fast, not silent

No retries, no fallbacks. If Docker isn't running, emit the error at boot. If the sandbox image is missing, tell the user the exact command to build it. A silent degradation ('sandbox unavailable, running on host') is worse than a failure because the user thinks they're protected when they aren't.

## Storage

### SQLite needs WAL plus busy_timeout actually applied

modernc/sqlite ignores ?_journal_mode=WAL&_busy_timeout=5000 DSN args silently. Pragmas must go via ?_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)&_pragma=busy_timeout(30000) or explicit Exec('PRAGMA ...') post-open. Verify PRAGMA journal_mode returns wal at startup and fail to boot if it doesn't — a silent revert to rollback mode turns every concurrent write into instant SQLITE_BUSY.
sources.verification_section:
## Verification

End-to-end smoke:

1. task build — clean across all modules (rrc plus core plus service plus web).

2. task test ./... — clean. New tests required: rrc/predicate_test.go for predicate composition and lowering. service/search/sqlitevec_oracle_test.go for NearestChunks returns top-K under various predicates with recall vs full-scan baseline above 0.95. core/adapter/zerank/zerank_test.go for adapter HTTP shape, sigmoid math, logprob extraction. core/adapter/zembed/zembed_test.go for adapter HTTP shape, asymmetric routing (query vs document endpoints), L2-normalization confirmation.

3. docker compose up -d — spidey-vllm-1 plus spidey-zembed-1 come up. Healthchecks green.

4. spidey-web boots. Settings JSON reflects new providers: classifier=zerank, embedder=zembed.

5. Invariance test: insert N messages of varying sizes synthetically, measure per-OnMessage time at N=100, N=1000, N=10000. Time should be flat (95th percentile within 1.5x across sizes). If linear, the cosine math wasn't actually deleted or the index isn't being used.

6. Reranker quality test: re-run rerank_eval/run_eval_v2.py against the live spidey-vllm-1 endpoint (not just isolated model). zerank-2 results should match the standalone numbers (~24/25 top-1).

7. Embedder quality test: re-run rerank_eval/run_eval_embed_v2.py against the live spidey-zembed-1 endpoint. zembed-1 results should match the standalone numbers (22/25 stage 1, 25/25 recall@10).

8. Filter test: insert chunks across 3 threads; query with PredScope(currentThread=t1, scope=all-threads) returns chunks from all threads; query with PredScope(currentThread=t1, scope=thread) returns only t1 chunks; recall measured via known plants in each thread.

9. Subagent test: spawn a subagent thread; verify oracle.NearestChunks returns chunks from the parent's history; subagent's edge formation persists to the same DAG (or its fork view) without corrupting the parent's view.

Specific observable that confirms the invariance promise: add index_ms, rerank_ms, embed_query_ms, embed_doc_ms decomposition to the OnMessage log line. Run a fresh thread to N=100 messages, then to N=1000. Verify index_ms stays roughly constant; only embed_*_ms (proportional to new chunks, independent of N) and rerank_ms (proportional to RerankTopK, independent of N) scale meaningfully. The old cosine_ms (flat-scan) field disappears entirely.

### Tests that pin the invariance contract

rrc/engine_invariance_test.go (new): synthetic corpus at sizes [100, 1000, 10000]; assert OnMessage wall time stays within a tight band across sizes (e.g., 95th percentile within 1.5x of the smallest). service/search/sqlitevec_oracle_test.go: explicit assertion that NearestChunks does not perform a table scan: query plan inspection or row-count instrumentation.
sources.quantization_arc_journal:
### Phase 9: Live verification arc — discovered hard hardware constraint

Brought up the docker stack:

1. docker compose build vllm zembed — both images built. zembed pre-downloaded model at build time.

2. docker compose up -d vllm zembed — both started.

3. zembed reached healthy quickly (model already in image).

4. vLLM crashed at boot: ValueError: Free memory on device cuda:0 (8.64/12.0 GiB) on startup is less than desired GPU memory utilization (0.92, 11.04 GiB). Decrease GPU memory utilization or reduce GPU memory used by other processes.

The architectural finding I'd missed: zembed-1 (4B, ~8GB at bf16) plus zerank-2 (4B, ~8GB at bf16) totals ~16GB just for model weights, on a 12GB GPU. The reranker eval and embedder eval each ran one model at a time (we explicitly stopped containers between). The plan implicitly assumed both could run simultaneously, and this was never measured.

### The quantization spiral

User chose: quantize both. Walked through the configurations:

vLLM --gpu-memory-utilization 0.4: model didn't fit at all. vLLM's utilization is a fraction of TOTAL VRAM (12GB times 0.4 = 4.8GB), zerank-2 at bf16 needs ~8GB so can't load.

zerank-2 with vLLM --quantization bitsandbytes --load-format bitsandbytes (int8): model loaded at 2.65 GiB, but zembed at bf16 was hogging the rest. No room for KV cache blocks.

Bumped vLLM utilization to 0.65, zembed still bf16: zembed had grown to ~8.5GB (more than the bf16 estimate — sentence-transformers plus transformers overhead, bnb instrumentation, fragmentation). vLLM still couldn't allocate KV cache.

Switch zembed to int8 via BitsAndBytesConfig load_in_8bit=True: zembed runtime memory still came in around 6-8GB despite the int8 weight estimate of ~4GB. PyTorch peak allocator plus sentence-transformers buffers eat more than the static weight calculation suggests.

Switch zembed to NF4 (4-bit) via BitsAndBytesConfig load_in_4bit=True bnb_4bit_quant_type=nf4 bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16: zembed memory dropped to ~2GB. vLLM at 0.6 utilization (~7.2GB) successfully loaded zerank-2 int8 plus compiled CUDA graphs (~0.89GB overhead) plus allocated KV cache (2.81 GiB, 20,432 tokens, 2.49x max concurrency at 8192-token requests).

API server still booting, curl /health returning 000. Then user's system froze.

User aborted: 'kill it we're aborting' and 'We can't run these two… its unviable. my system frozed up.'

### Architectural finding (load-bearing)

The substrate plan claimed zembed-1 plus zerank-2 fit on a 12GB consumer GPU. They don't. Even with aggressive quantization (NF4 4-bit zembed plus int8 zerank), the combined runtime memory at inference plus KV cache is at the system's edge — and 'at the edge' includes cases where the host system is destabilized by GPU memory pressure (the freeze is the signal).

### Tests that pin the invariance contract

rrc/engine_invariance_test.go (new): synthetic corpus at sizes [100, 1000, 10000]; assert OnMessage wall time stays within a tight band across sizes (e.g., 95th percentile within 1.5x of the smallest). service/search/sqlitevec_oracle_test.go: explicit assertion that NearestChunks does not perform a table scan: query plan inspection or row-count instrumentation.

pairs.query: what bitsandbytes configuration finally allowed zembed to drop to ~2GB
pairs.correct_source:
### Phase 9: Live verification arc — discovered hard hardware constraint

Brought up the docker stack:

1. docker compose build vllm zembed — both images built. zembed pre-downloaded model at build time.

2. docker compose up -d vllm zembed — both started.

3. zembed reached healthy quickly (model already in image).

4. vLLM crashed at boot: ValueError: Free memory on device cuda:0 (8.64/12.0 GiB) on startup is less than desired GPU memory utilization (0.92, 11.04 GiB). Decrease GPU memory utilization or reduce GPU memory used by other processes.

The architectural finding I'd missed: zembed-1 (4B, ~8GB at bf16) plus zerank-2 (4B, ~8GB at bf16) totals ~16GB just for model weights, on a 12GB GPU. The reranker eval and embedder eval each ran one model at a time (we explicitly stopped containers between). The plan implicitly assumed both could run simultaneously, and this was never measured.

### The quantization spiral

User chose: quantize both. Walked through the configurations:

vLLM --gpu-memory-utilization 0.4: model didn't fit at all. vLLM's utilization is a fraction of TOTAL VRAM (12GB times 0.4 = 4.8GB), zerank-2 at bf16 needs ~8GB so can't load.

zerank-2 with vLLM --quantization bitsandbytes --load-format bitsandbytes (int8): model loaded at 2.65 GiB, but zembed at bf16 was hogging the rest. No room for KV cache blocks.

Bumped vLLM utilization to 0.65, zembed still bf16: zembed had grown to ~8.5GB (more than the bf16 estimate — sentence-transformers plus transformers overhead, bnb instrumentation, fragmentation). vLLM still couldn't allocate KV cache.

Switch zembed to int8 via BitsAndBytesConfig load_in_8bit=True: zembed runtime memory still came in around 6-8GB despite the int8 weight estimate of ~4GB. PyTorch peak allocator plus sentence-transformers buffers eat more than the static weight calculation suggests.

Switch zembed to NF4 (4-bit) via BitsAndBytesConfig load_in_4bit=True bnb_4bit_quant_type=nf4 bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16: zembed memory dropped to ~2GB. vLLM at 0.6 utilization (~7.2GB) successfully loaded zerank-2 int8 plus compiled CUDA graphs (~0.89GB overhead) plus allocated KV cache (2.81 GiB, 20,432 tokens, 2.49x max concurrency at 8192-token requests).

API server still booting, curl /health returning 000. Then user's system froze.

User aborted: 'kill it we're aborting' and 'We can't run these two… its unviable. my system frozed up.'

### Architectural finding (load-bearing)

The substrate plan claimed zembed-1 plus zerank-2 fit on a 12GB consumer GPU. They don't. Even with aggressive quantization (NF4 4-bit zembed plus int8 zerank), the combined runtime memory at inference plus KV cache is at the system's edge — and 'at the edge' includes cases where the host system is destabilized by GPU memory pressure (the freeze is the signal).
